title: Project and Research Boundary
description: Start with the README to understand the four-stage Explainable Diabetes Risk Digital Twin and the role each stage plays. It also establishes the project's essential safety boundary: predictions, SHAP values, simulated scenarios, graph relationships, and 3D twins are model-derived research outputs, not diagnosis, treatment advice, or causal evidence.

title: Shared Diabetes Vocabulary
description: With the research goal clear, study the shared BRFSS feature schema, three-class risk labels, artifact paths, patient validation, and model-loading helpers. This module is the common vocabulary that keeps training, dashboard inference, SHAP explanation, simulation, and graph evidence aligned around the same patient record.
languageLesson: Python modules can act as a single source of truth by centralizing constants, validation, and serialization helpers; every stage imports the same definitions instead of duplicating feature logic.

title: Stages 1 and 2
description: Building on the shared schema, the training script produces the class-balanced three-class model and evaluation artifacts, while the notebook provides the reproducible research narrative for training, class-imbalance-aware evaluation, global importance, and patient-level SHAP. Read these together to see how model evidence is created before the dashboard consumes it, and why balanced accuracy, macro-F1, per-class behavior, and non-causal interpretation matter alongside raw accuracy.

title: Dashboard Orchestration
description: The Flask entry point turns the research pipeline into one dataset-backed patient journey. It coordinates stable numbered-patient selection, prediction, SHAP evidence, Stage 3 comparison, separate current and scenario twins, and temporary Stage 4 graph delivery, making it the best bird's-eye view of runtime control flow.
languageLesson: Flask route functions form the HTTP boundary, while lazy singleton loading delays expensive model and twin initialization until a request actually needs those resources.

title: Stage 3 Simulation
description: From the dashboard, Stage 3 creates a model-backed Digital Twin for the current patient and a manual what-if profile changed only through explicit inputs. The module preserves three-class probabilities and SHAP-compatible explanations while framing differences as non-causal model responses rather than predicted treatment effects.

title: Patient-Specific 3D Twins
description: The twin generator converts each profile's BMI and model risk into SMPL body-shape and colour parameters, so the current and scenario models are generated independently from their own inputs. Its lazy handling of licensed legacy weights keeps the dashboard usable when optional SMPL assets are unavailable and separates numerical model evidence from visual representation.
languageLesson: Optional heavyweight Python dependencies are commonly loaded lazily and guarded with explicit fallbacks, allowing the core application to run even when visualization-only assets are absent.

title: Stage 4 Evidence Graph
description: Stage 4 assembles a complete patient-centric, explain-only graph containing decoded observations, all patient-specific SHAP contributions, three probabilities, and the current Digital Twin. Reusable definitions and model metadata may live in Neo4j, but patient evidence remains an in-memory DTO and avoids invented direct causal edges from observations to diabetes risk.

title: Browser Experience
description: The Jinja template unifies patient import and selection with the four stages, while the Cytoscape script turns Stage 4's DTO into an inspectable and filterable evidence graph. Together they reveal how the backend's patient-consistency rules and research limitations are communicated in the browser rather than remaining hidden in Python code.
languageLesson: Server-rendered Jinja establishes the initial page structure, then client-side JavaScript progressively enhances the delivered graph data with Cytoscape layout, filtering, inspection, and responsive relayout.

title: Evidence and Boundary Tests
description: After seeing the full flow, use the Stage 4 tests to verify that the graph is complete, faithful to probabilities and SHAP values, idempotent, and safe when Neo4j is unavailable. These checks also protect the temporary patient-data boundary, making the project's explain-only claims executable rather than merely documented.

title: Reproducible Docker Workflow
description: The shared Docker image packages the Python, machine-learning, Jupyter, Neo4j-client, and optional SMPL requirements used by the earlier steps. Docker Compose then orchestrates the Flask dashboard, Jupyter workflows, Neo4j, notebook execution, and mesh export with localhost-only ports, while the example environment file supplies reusable graph credentials without storing patient data.
languageLesson: Docker Compose defines cooperating services, shared images, health-aware dependencies, ports, volumes, and environment variables in one reproducible YAML workflow; keeping data services separate from the web process also makes fallback behavior testable.

title: Operate and Demonstrate
description: Finish with the user and supervisor guides, which translate the architecture into a repeatable demonstration: start the stack, choose one numbered dataset patient, interpret Stages 1-4, compare a manual scenario, and disclose limitations. This final stop reconnects every implementation layer to the project's research question and ensures the system is presented as evidence-backed decision-support research rather than a clinical product.
